title: Restore ovarian endocrine function without previously banked tissue

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to restore an ovarian system that produces appropriately regulated hormone cycles after substantial follicle loss, without relying on ovarian tissue saved before that loss. The central goal is sustained endocrine function. Restoring fertility would be an additional achievement requiring competent oocytes and successful reproductive outcomes; hormone recovery alone would not establish it.

Conceptual distinction: activating follicles that remain, generating new functional follicles, and transplanting previously banked ovarian tissue address different biological starting conditions. Activating a residual pool would depend on follicles still being present and would not by itself establish replenishment. Generating new follicles would require creating functional reproductive units. Stored-tissue transplantation supplies follicles preserved earlier. The supplied clinical evidence demonstrates the last approach, which provides a comparator for the proposed innovation.

significance.text: Successful restoration without prior tissue banking would remove a major prerequisite of the documented transplantation approach. People who lack stored tissue could potentially recover cyclic ovarian endocrine function after substantial loss or failure. The Bologna study explicitly included endocrine restoration as a treatment goal separate from a desire for pregnancy, illustrating why this capability could matter independently of fertility.

Conditional impact synthesis: if treatment also restored functional follicles containing competent oocytes, it could expand reproductive options. This would require separate evidence of reproductive competence, pregnancies and healthy births. Endocrine recovery does not automatically establish fertility, and reproductive success does not establish durable recipient or offspring safety.

Impact boundary: recovery of ovarian function should not be equated with reversing reproductive aging generally or guaranteeing better long-term health. Effects on cancer risk, cardiovascular outcomes and other health measures would require direct follow-up. The significance of the proposed advance rests first on the specific endocrine capability demonstrated, with broader benefits remaining conditional.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is sustained, appropriately regulated ovarian endocrine restoration after substantial follicle loss without previously banked ovarian tissue. The supplied sources do not demonstrate this capability, but they also do not establish that it remained unavailable across the field as of 2026-11-01. Neither residual-follicle activation nor generation of new follicles is evaluated by the supplied clinical study.

Engineering synthesis: the barriers depend on the biological starting point. An approach that activates remaining follicles must establish that an adequate residual pool exists, demonstrate meaningful recovery and determine its duration. An approach that creates new follicles must establish functional organization and coordination between the oocyte and its supporting cells. Neither approach can be inferred to work merely because transplanted stored tissue functions.

Engineering synthesis: endocrine restoration requires coordinated hormone production and physiological feedback over time. A transient rise in hormone concentration or a return of bleeding would provide narrower evidence. If fertility is claimed, additional barriers include oocyte maturation and developmental competence. Safe implementation must also address treatment-specific risks and establish whether function persists without repeated intervention.

current_state.text: The Bologna University report published on 7 March 2024 describes a single-center retrospective experience with transplantation of previously cryopreserved ovarian tissue in selected cancer survivors. It reports endocrine recovery, pregnancies and live births. These findings demonstrate restoration using stored tissue, rather than regeneration after depletion without a stored supply. Some tissue was collected after chemotherapy, so the entire cohort should not be characterized as having banked tissue before all gonadotoxic treatment.

The detailed results report endocrine recovery in 18 of 20 women with premature ovarian insufficiency evaluated after at least six months. Endocrine assessment included hormonal assays, follicular growth and return of menstruation. The reproductive results report ten pregnancies among 26 women, comprising four live births, two pregnancies ongoing at reporting and four spontaneous abortions. The abstract and body use differing pregnancy denominators, and some aggregate discussion percentages are inconsistent with the detailed counts. These reporting issues limit precise rate interpretation without negating the documented occurrence of endocrine recovery and reproductive outcomes.

The selected retrospective cohort does not establish universal success, comparative effectiveness or long-term safety. The report also discusses the risk of reintroducing cancer cells with transplanted tissue, reinforcing the need for treatment-specific safety evaluation. Its outcomes support the biological goal of restoring ovarian function but cannot validate a method that does not use previously stored tissue.

The research summary identifies a review dated 28 September 2024 concerning ovarian tissue banking and transplantation to delay natural menopause, and reports an earlier abstract inspection. However, the retained copy available to the validated review contained only a cookie-access message, with no scientific text or independently confirmable article identity. Accordingly, this record cannot establish the proposal’s evidence base or clinical efficacy from that citation. The extraction failure is an evidence limitation, not evidence that the proposal is ineffective.

Evidence boundary: the supplied search record is empty and does not establish the field’s status as of 2026-11-01. The dated transplantation findings therefore should not be read as a comprehensive account of later developments, nor as proof that restoration without previously banked tissue remains unavailable.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: controlled human studies, independently replicated, would show sustained ovarian endocrine function without previously banked ovarian tissue in clearly characterized participants. Protocols should specify the cause and extent of ovarian dysfunction, evidence of residual follicles, prior treatments and any concurrent hormonal support. Results should distinguish recovery supported by remaining follicles from claims of newly generated follicles.
completion_criteria.label: Independently replicated sustained endocrine recovery without previously banked ovarian tissue

completion_criteria.text: Proposed assessment: repeated hormonal measurements, evidence of follicular activity and menstrual-cycle observations could build on endpoints used in the transplantation study. A convincing protocol would additionally define physiological regulation, duration, consistency of function and dependence on further treatment. These are proposed evaluation requirements; the supplied publication does not establish a universal completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Endocrine assessment defines physiological regulation, durability, and treatment dependence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed fertility assessment: a fertility claim would require evidence of viable, developmentally competent oocytes and successful reproductive outcomes, including healthy births. Long-term follow-up of recipients and offspring would remain necessary. Cancer, cardiovascular and other health effects should be measured directly rather than inferred from restored hormones or pregnancies.
completion_criteria.label: Fertility claims demonstrate competent oocytes, healthy births, and long-term follow-up

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: studies should report response rates, failures, duration of benefit, repeat-treatment requirements and adverse outcomes by patient subgroup. Independent replication should test whether results extend beyond a single center or narrowly selected population. Finite studies can establish demonstrated breadth across specified conditions, not literal universality across all causes of ovarian failure or all recipients.
completion_criteria.label: Report subgroup-specific treatment outcomes and independently replicated breadth of benefit

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: END-02, a general platform for replacing failed endocrine glands with feedback-responsive tissue, is the closest platform-level overlap. END-08 addresses the distinct ovarian capability and could succeed without establishing replacement methods for other glands. Conversely, a general gland platform would still need to demonstrate ovarian cycle regulation and, for fertility claims, competent oocytes.

Roster-based synthesis: END-01 concerns renewable, immune-protected human islets, while END-07 concerns regeneration of a person’s own pancreatic beta cells. Both share the goal of restoring endogenous endocrine function. Their cell types and glucose-control endpoints differ from the ovarian follicular system and its separate endocrine and reproductive endpoints.

Roster-based synthesis: END-03, continuous monitoring of multiple hormones, could support assessment of restored ovarian dynamics. END-04, a predictive theory of interacting endocrine control systems, overlaps with understanding physiological regulation. END-06, tissue-selective control of hormone action, concerns where hormones act rather than restoration of their ovarian source. These capabilities could assist END-08 without establishing it.

Roster-based synthesis: END-05 targets dysfunctional energy-balance regulation, and END-09 targets glucose-responsive insulin dosing. They share an interest in durable physiological control but address different functions and mechanisms. END-10, antigen-specific tolerance in autoimmune endocrine disease, could be relevant where autoimmunity causes ovarian dysfunction; immune tolerance alone would not demonstrate replacement of follicles already lost. END-08 also overlaps with fertility treatment, regenerative medicine and cancer survivorship while retaining endocrine restoration as its central endpoint.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish whether any approach achieved the target capability by 2026-11-01 or afterward.
The natural-menopause review’s scientific content and the earlier abstract-based characterization cannot be independently confirmed from the retained cookie-access page.
Differences between abstract and body pregnancy denominators, and inconsistent aggregate percentages in the Bologna report, remain unresolved.
The supplied evidence does not evaluate residual-follicle activation or generation of new functional follicles.

A future demonstration protocol must define eligible populations, physiological regulation, required duration, concurrent treatment allowances and safety endpoints; no numerical completion thresholds are established here.
Durable endocrine benefit, fertility, offspring outcomes and long-term cancer or cardiovascular effects of the proposed innovation remain separate unanswered questions.

brief.title: Restored hormone cycles without tissue saved earlier
possible: People whose ovaries have lost much of their egg supply could regain lasting, naturally regulated hormone cycles, even if they never froze ovarian tissue for later use.
why: This would open a path to hormone recovery for people who lack stored tissue. That could matter independently of whether they want to become pregnant.

sources.who: Raffaella Fabbri and colleagues at the University of Bologna
sources.showed: A study looking back at selected cancer survivors found that transplanting their previously frozen ovarian tissue restored hormone function and led to live births.
sources.quote: recovery of endocrine function was observed in all but one woman who underwent orthotopic transplantation
sources.cited_for: Transplanted stored tissue can restore ovarian hormone production.
sources.not_established: The study does not demonstrate recovery without previously stored tissue or establish long-term safety.

sources.showed: The authors reviewed freezing and transplanting ovarian tissue as a possible way to delay menopause. They concluded that this use remains clinically unproven.
sources.cited_for: Stored-tissue transplantation is being considered as a way to delay menopause.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish that transplantation delays menopause or restores ovarian function without stored tissue.

shown: A team at the University of Bologna reported hormone recovery and live births after transplanting previously frozen ovarian tissue. Their study followed a small, selected group at a single center. It demonstrates what stored tissue can do; recovery after major egg loss without that supply remains a separate goal.
missing: Controlled human studies must demonstrate sustained ovarian hormone recovery without previously banked tissue, with independent teams reproducing the result.
Recovery must include coordinated hormone cycles over time, beyond a brief hormone rise or a return of bleeding.
Treatments must distinguish activating surviving follicles, the structures containing eggs and supporting cells, from creating new ones.
Studies must establish how long benefits last, whether treatment must be repeated, and which patients benefit safely.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce lasting recovery without stored tissue
milestones.explanation: Controlled human studies would have to reproduce sustained hormone recovery without banked tissue in clearly described patients, distinguishing surviving from newly formed follicles. This would establish the central capability.

milestones.label: Hormone cycles show lasting physiological regulation
milestones.explanation: Repeated hormone tests, follicle activity and menstrual observations would have to establish normal regulation, duration, consistency and dependence on further treatment. This would distinguish durable function from a temporary response.

milestones.label: Fertility claims establish healthy births and long-term outcomes
milestones.explanation: Fertility claims would require eggs capable of healthy development, healthy births and long-term follow-up of recipients and children, including direct health assessments. Hormone recovery alone would not establish these outcomes.

milestones.label: Benefits and failures are reproduced across patient groups
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to report successes, failures, duration, repeat treatments and harms by patient group. This would establish who benefits and under which conditions.

uncertain: How much surviving follicle tissue would a treatment need, and could an approach instead create new functional follicles?
What duration and pattern of hormone recovery should count as success, and how much ongoing treatment would be acceptable?
Would restored cycles support fertility or change long-term cancer and heart health risks?

page.title: Ovarian endocrine regeneration after follicle loss
page.definition: After follicle loss, the ovary resumes cyclic production of estradiol and progesterone. The pituitary gland signals the ovary, and ovarian hormones in turn regulate those signals. Follicles contain immature eggs and supporting cells. Recovery may use surviving follicles or newly formed ones. Transplantation can restore ovarian function using previously frozen tissue or fresh donor tissue. Regeneration would achieve recovery without either.

goal.need: Recent estimates place premature ovarian insufficiency unrelated to medical treatment at 3.5% of women. Loss of ovarian activity before age 40 can cause hot flashes and bone loss. Hormone therapy relieves symptoms and protects bone and is generally recommended until the usual age of menopause. Sustained recovery could relieve symptoms and reduce years of replacement therapy for women without stored tissue or a donor. Treatments that reactivate follicles require some to survive. Fertility is a separate outcome.

completion.title: FDA approves restoration of cyclic ovarian hormone production without stored or donor ovarian tissue.
completion.criterion: FDA approves a new drug application, a biologics license application or an efficacy supplement for restoration of cyclic endogenous ovarian estradiol and progesterone production after ovarian insufficiency or follicle loss, without previously stored or donated ovarian tissue. The approved labeling must support that indication in the population and over the duration claimed.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, drug approval, biologics licensing and efficacy supplement requirements applied to the proposed indication.
completion.threshold_quote: an efficacy supplement to an NDA or BLA for a new indication
completion.basis: Marketing authorization is an externally adjudicated test of the claimed therapeutic effect, safety and manufacturing. FDA’s published requirements apply to the proposed indication; they do not supply an ovarian-specific hormone concentration, cycle count or duration threshold. Fresh donor transplantation is already demonstrated and is excluded from the regenerative capability defined here.

milestones.title: Treated rats recover estrous cycling and show improved hormone levels after chemotherapy injury.
milestones.criterion: In rats with cyclophosphamide-induced ovarian injury, vaginal smears show improved estrous cycling relative to injured controls. Serum estradiol and anti-Müllerian hormone are higher and follicle-stimulating hormone is lower in treated rats than in injured controls. The study uses one-way analysis of variance with p < 0.05 for the hormone comparisons.
milestones.set_by: Atlas applies the endpoints and statistical cutoff of Ai and colleagues’ rat experiment. No external body was identified that defines this combination as a preclinical success standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: p value < 0.05 was significant in statistical analysis results.

milestones.title: An FDA investigational new drug application takes effect for an ovarian-restoration treatment.
milestones.criterion: An investigational new drug application covering human administration of the ovarian-restoration candidate becomes effective. FDA permits this 30 days after receiving the application unless it imposes a clinical hold, or earlier following notification that investigations may begin. Supporting nonclinical information must characterize safety sufficiently for the proposed starting dose and study design. This establishes permission for human testing.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Phase 1 IND Frequently Asked Questions, sections 2 and 9, implementing 21 CFR 312.
milestones.threshold_quote: The IND may go into effect 30 days after FDA receives the application

milestones.title: An ovarian-restoration treatment is administered to people with 12 months of safety follow-up.
milestones.criterion: Recipients with idiopathic premature ovarian insufficiency receive the intraovarian intervention and complete safety follow-up through 12 months. Monitor acute procedural complications during the first 24 hours and first week. Assess later complications, including ovarian abscesses and benign neoplasms, by physical examination and vaginal ultrasonography at the protocol follow-up visits.
milestones.set_by: Royan Institute investigators, phase I study NCT02603744 and its published protocol; written for idiopathic POI and retrospectively registered on 13 November 2015.
milestones.threshold_quote: for 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months after the transplantation to evaluate safety and effectiveness, and any secondary complications.

milestones.title: An ovarian treatment improves natural cycles and follicle activity versus placebo over 24 weeks.
milestones.criterion: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial over 24 weeks, the treated group has more natural menstrual cycles and greater residual follicle activity than the placebo group at two-sided p < 0.05. Count only menstruation associated with endogenous progesterone, excluding bleeding induced by administered progestogen. Assess follicle activity by serial transvaginal ultrasound using the modified Hoogland–Skouby score for each 28-day period. The registered protocol specifies 102 participants.
milestones.set_by: Guangdong Provincial Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine investigators, registered HYYK protocol ChiCTR2100049604; written for residual-follicle activity in women aged 18–42 diagnosed with POI before 40.
milestones.threshold_quote: Only natural menstruation, influenced by endogenous progesterone, is acknowledged as a valid outcome marker.

milestones.title: Expanded clinical studies establish ovarian endocrine recovery and its treatment benefit–risk balance.
milestones.criterion: The candidate produces effectiveness and safety evidence in expanded phase 3 studies sufficient to evaluate its overall benefit–risk relationship for the ovarian endocrine restoration indication and support prescribing information. Restoration endpoints, follow-up and eligible populations must be those of the candidate’s clinical development programme. FDA’s phase 3 definition supplies no mandatory sample size, hormone concentration, cycle count or duration.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Drug Development and Review Definitions, Phase 3 Clinical Studies; the definition applies generally to drug development.
milestones.threshold_quote: and are intended to gather the additional information about effectiveness and safety that is needed to evaluate the overall benefit-risk relationship of the drug.

milestones.title: FDA accepts an application for substantive review of an ovarian endocrine restoration indication.
milestones.criterion: FDA accepts for filing a new drug application, biologics license application or efficacy supplement seeking the ovarian endocrine restoration indication. The proposed use must cover recovery of cyclic endogenous ovarian hormone production without previously stored or donated ovarian tissue. The filing decision establishes that the application is sufficiently complete for substantive review.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, CDER 21st Century Review Process Desk Reference Guide, section 3.2.1, and CBER biologics license application requirements.
milestones.threshold_quote: The goal of the filing review is to determine whether the application, on its face, is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review.

not_found: No ovarian-specific regulatory standard defining restoration by hormone concentrations, endogenous cycle count and duration was found.
No verified FDA marketing authorization or qualifying phase 3 result for ovarian endocrine regeneration was found.
No controlled human demonstration of endocrine restoration through newly generated follicles or after verified complete follicle depletion was found.
No public FDA decision authorizing an ovarian-restoration IND was verified.
ClinicalTrials.gov records NCT02603744 and NCT02372474 opened without study text; the published reports supplied the cited trial information.

edit m4: criterion = "In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial over 24 weeks, the treated group has more natural menstrual cycles and greater residual follicle activity than the placebo group at two-sided p < 0.05. Count only menstruation associated with endogenous progesterone, excluding bleeding induced by administered progestogen. Assess follicle activity by serial transvaginal ultrasound using the modified Hoogland\u2013Skouby score for each 28-day period. The registered protocol specifies 102 participants."; threshold_quote = "Only natural menstruation, influenced by endogenous progesterone, is acknowledged as a valid outcome marker."; threshold_ref = 10; refs = [10].
